name: Interdigital Webbing Extension
description: Extends the vestigial webbing between human fingers and toes into functional swimming membranes. The webbing is thin, translucent, and vascularized, extending to approximately two-thirds of the finger length. It dramatically improves swimming speed and efficiency — a webbed swimmer moves through water with roughly twice the efficiency of an unmodified human. The webbing is retractable in premium installations (Zheng-Dao Bioelectric), folding against the fingers when not in use. Budget versions are permanent, which impacts fine motor tasks — typing, small-object manipulation, and tool use are all somewhat impaired. In Old Harbor, webbing is practical. In the corporate towers, permanent webbing is career-limiting. Retractable webbing is the compromise that lets aquatic workers maintain a foot in both worlds.
source_organism: Rana temporaria (common frog), Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris (capybara, partial webbing genes)
procedure: Hand and foot retroviral injection with membrane growth factor, 2 sessions
reversibility: Surgically removable; retractable versions can be gene-suppressed
side_effects: Permanent versions impair fine motor tasks
Webbing tears easily and heals slowly
Skin between fingers dries and cracks in arid environments
Gloves and tight shoes don't fit — custom sizing required
social_perception: Practical in maritime communities, quirky elsewhere. Permanent webbing is seen as a commitment to an aquatic lifestyle. Retractable webbing is considered clever engineering. Children find webbed hands fascinating.
story_hooks: A webbed swimmer discovers their membrane tissue is absorbing chemicals from the water and storing them — their hands are becoming a biological record of water pollution
A black-market webbing installation uses synthetic membrane tissue that contains a tracking compound — every stroke through water leaves a chemical trail
